papers.title_zh: 通过分子动力学和自由能分析对 LipL32 靶向 DNA 适体进行结构引导优化
papers.source_body_en: Abstract Accurate detection of leptospirosis requires high-affinity recognition of the conserved LipL32 biomarker. Although LipL32-targeting DNA aptamers have been identified through systematic evolution of ligands by exponential enrichment (SELEX), the molecular basis of their target recognition remains unclear, limiting rational post-SELEX optimization. Here, we investigated the molecular recognition mechanism of the LepDapt-5 aptamer family using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and binding free-energy analysis. We generated three-dimensional aptamer models using AlphaFold 3 (AF3) and constructed protein–aptamer docking complexes with HADDOCK, showing a stable G-quadruplex (GQ) motif within the aptamer core. Structural and energetic analyses identified key domains contributing to LipL32 binding, while per-residue energy decomposition highlighted nucleotides suitable for rational sequence refinement. Guided by these insights, we introduced targeted single-point mutations, evaluated their effects computationally, and validated their performance experimentally using enzyme-linked aptamer sorbent assays (ELASA). Relative binding free energies (ΔΔGbind) calculated using nonequilibrium alchemical MD showed strong agreement with ELASA measurements: T19A reduced binding affinity, G7C produced minimal change, and G24C significantly enhanced affinity. Experimental equilibrium dissociation constants (KD) further supported these predictions, identifying G24C as the highest-affinity variant. Additionally, the G24C mutant retained strong binding to LipL32 while exhibiting no detectable binding to the NS1 protein of dengue virus 2 and the E2 protein of Chikungunya virus.

papers.title: Acute viral encephalitis syndrome in paediatric patients: Clinical profile and laboratory correlation
papers.abstract: Objectives: Acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) poses a significant public health challenge in India, particularly in children. The aetiological spectrum varies regionally, with viral agents being predominant. This study evaluates the clinico-virological profile of AES in children at a tertiary care centre in North Karnataka. Material and Methods: A prospective observational study was conducted among children aged 6 months to 12 years presenting with AES, defined as acute fever with altered sensorium and/or seizures. Detailed clinical evaluation, neuroimaging and laboratory investigations were performed. Immunoglobulin M enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay testing for herpes simplex virus type (HSV)-1, HSV-2, mumps, dengue, chikungunya and Japanese encephalitis (JE) virus was used to determine viral aetiology. Outcomes were assessed at discharge. Results: Among 41 children, 58.5% were male and most were from low socioeconomic backgrounds. Fever and altered sensorium were present in all cases; seizures occurred in 68.3%. Mumps (22%), HSV-1/2 (17%), dengue (14.6%) and JE (4.9%) were the major viral causes identified, while no aetiology could be determined in 51.2% of cases. Neuroimaging was abnormal in 34.2%, and hypoxia, low Glasgow Coma Scale and need for ventilation were associated with poorer outcomes. The mortality rate was 17%. Conclusion: A substantial proportion of AES cases remained aetiologically undiagnosed, underscoring the limitations of current diagnostic tools. Regional epidemiological data and enhanced viral testing are essential for developing targeted public health strategies, improving early detection and preventing long-term morbidity and mortality among affected children.

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: Acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) poses a significant public health challenge in India, particularly in children. The aetiological spectrum varies regionally, with viral agents being predominant.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: This study evaluates the clinico-virological profile of AES in children at a tertiary care centre in North Karnataka. A prospective observational study was conducted among children aged 6 months to 12 years presenting with AES, defined as acute fever with altered sensorium and/or seizures.
analysis_en.methods: Immunoglobulin M enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay testing for herpes simplex virus type (HSV)-1, HSV-2, mumps, dengue, chikungunya and Japanese encephalitis (JE) virus was used to determine viral aetiology. Outcomes were assessed at discharge.

Mumps (22%), HSV-1/2 (17%), dengue (14.6%) and JE (4.9%) were the major viral causes identified, while no aetiology could be determined in 51.2% of cases. analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: A substantial proportion of AES cases remained aetiologically undiagnosed, underscoring the limitations of current diagnostic tools.

papers.title_zh: 儿科患者急性病毒性脑炎综合征:临床特征和实验室相关性
papers.source_body_en: Objectives: Acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) poses a significant public health challenge in India, particularly in children. The aetiological spectrum varies regionally, with viral agents being predominant. This study evaluates the clinico-virological profile of AES in children at a tertiary care centre in North Karnataka. Material and Methods: A prospective observational study was conducted among children aged 6 months to 12 years presenting with AES, defined as acute fever with altered sensorium and/or seizures. Detailed clinical evaluation, neuroimaging and laboratory investigations were performed. Immunoglobulin M enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay testing for herpes simplex virus type (HSV)-1, HSV-2, mumps, dengue, chikungunya and Japanese encephalitis (JE) virus was used to determine viral aetiology. Outcomes were assessed at discharge. Results: Among 41 children, 58.5% were male and most were from low socioeconomic backgrounds. Fever and altered sensorium were present in all cases; seizures occurred in 68.3%. Mumps (22%), HSV-1/2 (17%), dengue (14.6%) and JE (4.9%) were the major viral causes identified, while no aetiology could be determined in 51.2% of cases. Neuroimaging was abnormal in 34.2%, and hypoxia, low Glasgow Coma Scale and need for ventilation were associated with poorer outcomes. The mortality rate was 17%. Conclusion: A substantial proportion of AES cases remained aetiologically undiagnosed, underscoring the limitations of current diagnostic tools. Regional epidemiological data and enhanced viral testing are essential for developing targeted public health strategies, improving early detection and preventing long-term morbidity and mortality among affected children.
papers.abstract_zh: 目标:急性脑炎综合征(AES)给印度带来了重大的公共卫生挑战,特别是对儿童而言。病因谱因地区而异,其中病毒因子占主导地位。本研究评估了北卡纳塔克邦三级护理中心儿童 AES 的临床病毒学特征。材料和方法:一项前瞻性观察研究在 6 个月至 12 岁患有 AES 的儿童中进行,AES 被定义为伴有感觉改变和/或癫痫发作的急性发烧。进行了详细的临床评估、神经影像学和实验室研究。采用免疫球蛋白 M 酶联免疫吸附测定法检测单纯疱疹病毒 (HSV)-1、HSV-2、腮腺炎、登革热、基孔肯雅热和日本脑炎 (JE) 病毒,以确定病毒病因。出院时评估结果。结果:41 名儿童中,58.5% 为男性,大多数社会经济背景较低。所有病例均出现发烧和感觉改变;68.3%发生癫痫发作。流行性腮腺炎 (22%)、HSV-1/2 (17%)、登革热 (14.6%) 和乙脑 (4.9%) 是确定的主要病毒原因,而 51.2% 的病例无法确定病因。34.2% 的患者神经影像学异常,缺氧、格拉斯哥昏迷评分低和需要通气与较差的预后相关。死亡率 率为 17%。结论:相当一部分 AES 病例的病因仍未得到诊断,这凸显了当前诊断工具的局限性。区域流行病学数据和加强病毒检测对于制定有针对性的公共卫生战略、改善早期发现并预防受影响儿童的长期发病和 死亡率 至关重要。

papers.title: Vector-Borne Disease Preparedness in Western North Carolina: Assessing Health Department Capacity for La Crosse Encephalitis Prevention and Response

source_records.title: Vector-Borne Disease Preparedness in Western North Carolina: Assessing Health Department Capacity for La Crosse Encephalitis Prevention and Response
Vector-Borne Disease Preparedness in Western North Carolina: Assessing Health Department Capacity for La Crosse Encephalitis Prevention and Response

papers.priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
papers.full_text: AbstractBACKGROUNDLa Crosse encephalitis (LACE), caused by La Crosse virus (LACV), is the leading cause of reported cases of pediatric arboviral encephalitis in the United States. However, mosquito-borne disease control capacity in Western North Carolina (WNC), where LACE is endemic, is poorly known.METHODSWe administered an electronic survey to communicable disease nurses (CDNs), environmental health specialists (EHS), and health directors in 10 WNC health departments with the highest reported incidence of LACE. The survey evaluated mosquito-borne disease knowledge and surveillance and control capacity based on respondent public health roles.RESULTSResponses were received from all surveyed health departments. A total of 47 public health professionals (16 CDNs, 23 EHS, and 8 health directors) completed the survey, resulting in a 36.7% response rate. One (10%) department was rated as “fully capable” based on national mosquito surveillance and control standards. Respondents identified gaps in knowledge of case definitions, serology interpretation, environmental and behavioral risk factors, and vector control capacity. Although most participants recognized the importance of preventing and controlling mosquito-borne disease, assessments of response capabilities varied by respondent job role.LIMITATIONSThis study was limited by sample size, moderate response rate, timing of the assessment, and reliance on self-reported data. Variability in job roles may have influenced how questions were interpreted.CONCLUSIONSThis study serves as a foundational assessment of mosquito-borne disease control capacity among health departments in WNC, where LACE remains a public health concern. Our findings highlight the need for improved preparedness through education and resources, and the findings also support a regional approach to strengthen prevention, detection, and response efforts.Keywords: La Crosse, encephalitis, mosquito, surveillance, vector-borne disease, Michael Ratliff, Sarah Brill Thach, Amy Lanou, Carl Williams, Brian Byrd MethodsThis study employed a cross-sectional survey to assess knowledge of vector-borne diseases and control capacity in 10 county-based health departments in WNC (Figure 1). These counties had the highest cumulative incidence of La Crosse encephalitis between 2000 and 2020.7 The primary data collection tool was an electronic survey developed using SurveyMonkey© software (San Mateo, CA). The survey contained 80 total items, including a combination of core questions administered to all participants and role-specific questions tailored to health directors, environmental health specialists, or communicable disease nurses. No individual respondent completed more than 32 questions. The full survey instrument is available from the corresponding author upon request.Figure 1.A) Map of the Study Area: Participating Western North Carolina Counties with the Highest Cumulative Incidence of Neuroinvasive La Crosse Virus Disease, 2000–2020; B) Respondents’ Ratings of Health Department Preparedness to Respond to Mosquito-Borne Disease CasesFigure note. Preparedness was assessed on a 7-point scale: 1 = extremely prepared and 7 = extremely unprepared. Respondents (N = 46) included local county health directors (HD, n = 8), communicable disease nurses (CDN, n = 16) and environmental health specialists (EHS, n = 22).A map of the state of turkey AI-generated content may be incorrect.The survey assessed vector-borne disease knowledge, perceptions of public health relevance, and existing mosquito surveillance and control capacity. Survey content assessing control capacity was structured around core and supplemental competencies recognized by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and adapted from the National Association of County and City Health Officials (NACCHO) framework for mosquito control programs.5 Because LACV is the most common mosquito-borne pathogen causing human disease in WNC, the scope of the survey was primarily focused on LACV and mosquito-borne disease response instead of other vector-borne diseases.The Office of Human Research Ethics at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill determined that this study did not meet the federal definition of human subjects research [45 CFR 46.102(e) or (l); 21 CFR 56.102(c), (e), or (l)] and therefore did not require Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval.Participants included health department directors, communicable disease nurses (CDNs), and registered environmental health specialists or interns (EHS). These specific job roles were selected as they have clearly defined roles as part of the public health response to “arboviral encephalitis/meningitis” as described in the local health department investigation steps within the North Carolina Communicable Disease Manual.22 Potential respondents were identified through a review of health department websites, the North Carolina State Board of Environmental Health Specialist Examiners registry, and professional contacts. The survey was distributed via email to 128 verified email addresses (10 health department directors, 18 CDNs, and 100 EHS). The survey remained open for 4 weeks (February 2024–March 2024), during which two reminder emails and follow-up phone calls were used to encourage participation.Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and contingency tables to compare vector-borne disease preparedness across roles. Basic data analyses (e.g., descriptive and summary statistics) were performed within the SurveyMonkey© website directly or exported to a .csv file for analyses using R/RStudio.23 Confidence intervals were calculated using the exact binomial method. Significance was defined a priori as P < .05 for all statistical tests. For paired ranking data, a global Friedman test was conducted first. When the Friedman test was statistically significant, pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were performed. Data visualizations and graphs were created using ggplot2 in R/RStudio.24 ResultsResponse RatesThe survey was distributed via email to 128 public health staff across 10 WNC local health departments. Of these, 62 individuals initiated the survey, and 60 individuals acknowledged the consent statement and identified their professional role as either a health director, environmental health specialist (EHS), or communicable disease nurse (CDN). Within individual counties, the number of respondents initiating the survey ranged from 2 to 12, (median: 6; mean: 6.7). A total of 47 participants completed the survey in full, resulting in an overall response rate of 36.7%. Public health personnel from all 10 health departments completed the survey, including 8 health directors, 23 EHS personnel, and 16 CDNs (the CDNs include 2 respondents that identified as public health nurses with communicable disease reporting or investigation responsibilities). Overall survey completion rates for specific job roles varied (80% of health directors, 23% of EHS, and 84.2% of CDNs); because individuals were allowed to skip questions during the survey, the responses to any single question may not equal the total number of participants.Health Department Preparedness to Respond to Mosquito-Borne DiseasesRespondents ranked their health department’s level of preparedness to respond to mosquito-borne disease cases, where 1 = extremely prepared, 2 = very prepared, 3 = somewhat prepared, 4 = unsure, 5 = somewhat unprepared, 6 = very unprepared, and 7 = extremely unprepared. Overall (N = 46), the median response was 3 (somewhat prepared) (mean: 3.63; range 2–7) (Figure 1). Although health directors responded more favorably (median: 2.5; mean: 2.9; range 2–5) and EHS personnel responded less favorably (median: 4; mean: 4.3; range 2–7), these differences were not statistically significant.Perceived Relative Importance of Mosquito-Borne DiseasesRespondents ranked selected mosquito-borne diseases in order of importance (public health relevance) for their respective counties (Figure 2). The choices included the following endemic and travel-related mosquito-borne diseases: eastern equine encephalitis, chikungunya virus disease, La Crosse encephalitis, malaria, St. Louis encephalitis, West Nile encephalitis, and Zika virus disease; the default order choice in the survey was alphabetical. La Crosse encephalitis (LACE) was overall ranked as the most important mosquito-borne disease of public health relevance (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Bonferroni correction, P < .01). Other endemic arboviral diseases, EEE and West Nile encephalitis, were ranked second and third, respectively, in terms of public health importance. This trend was consistent when evaluated by professional job category; however, pairwise comparisons were not significantly different for LACE and EEE (P > .05) for health directors, CDNs, or EHS. Pairwise comparisons suggest that LACE was ranked higher than the remaining mosquito-borne diseases by CDNs and EHS personnel; the small sample size for health directors limits statistical inference.Figure 2.Ranked Importance of Selected Mosquito-Borne DiseasesFigure note. Respondent rankings (1 = most important, 7 = least important), of seven travel-related or endemic mosquito-borne diseases in order of public health relevance. Rankings are presented collectively (A) and by personnel job type (B–D). Ranked choices included eastern equine encephalitis (EEE), chikungunya virus disease (CVD), La Crosse encephalitis (LACE), malaria, St. Louis encephalitis (SLE), West Nile encephalitis (WNE), and Zika virus disease (ZVD).A diagram of a health care worker AI-generated content may be incorrect.Mosquito Surveillance and Control CapacityHealth department directors and EHS personnel reported their respective health department’s mosquito surveillance and control capacities (Table 1) in the context of a comprehensive evidence-based mosquito control program using standards developed by NACCHO and the CDC. The 5 core capacities developed by NACCHO include 1) routine surveillance, standardized trapping, and identifications; 2) treatment decisions using surveillance data; 3) larviciding, adulticiding, or both; 4) routine vector control; and 5) pesticide resistance testing. The percentage of health departments reporting existing capacity for the individual core standards ranged from 10% to 40%, with one county reporting existing capacity for all 5 core standards. The most common standard (i.e., treatment decisions using surveillance data) existed in 40% of the counties; 20% of counties reported routine surveillance or routine vector control. A single county reported pesticide resistance testing. Health departments reporting existing capacity for the individual supplemental standards ranged from 10% to 50%. The most common supplemental capacity (community outreach and education activities) was reported in 50% of the counties. A single health director reported “in house” personnel with a pesticide applicator’s license. One of 10 counties reported existing capacity for all 5 supplemental standards; this county had all 5 core capacities as well.Table 1.National Standards for Mosquito Surveillance and Control Capabilities in 10 Western North Carolina (WNC) Health Departments A) Core Capacity Standards Counties with Standard (%) B) Supplemental Capacity Standards Counties with Standard (%) 1. Routine surveillance, standardized trapping, and identifications20%1. Licensed pesticide application requirements10%2. Treatment decisions using surveillance data40%2. Non-chemical vector control30%3. Larviciding, adulticiding, or both20%3. Community outreach and education activities50%4. Routine vector control20%4. Communication with local health departments on surveillance and epidemiology30%5. Pesticide resistance testing10%5. Cooperation with partner vector control programs50%Counties with all 5 core capacities10%a Counties with all 5 supplemental capacities10%a a One surveyed Western North Carolina (WNC) county has all the core standards and supplemental capacities.Knowledge of Risk Factors for La Crosse EncephalitisTo evaluate the knowledge of health department personnel regarding risk factors increasing transmission risk, environmental health specialists (EHS) and communicable disease nurses (CDN) were surveyed using questions designed to assess their understanding of environmental and behavioral risk factors associated with mosquito-borne diseases in general, and La Crosse encephalitis specifically.CDN and EHS personnel were surveyed to assess their knowledge of potential environmental risk factors associated with La Crosse encephalitis (LACE) (Table 2). A large majority (≥ 75%) of CDNs correctly identified 5 out of 6 environmental risk factors known to specifically increase the risk of LACE. However, 56.2% recognized the absence of air conditioning at a residence as a risk factor. All CDN respondents (n = 16) misidentified a “pond near residence” as a LACE risk factor, and 68.75% misidentified “creek near residence” as a risk factor. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractBACKGROUNDLa Crosse encephalitis (LACE), caused by La Crosse virus (LACV), is the leading cause of reported cases of pediatric arboviral encephalitis in the United States. However, mosquito-borne disease control capacity in Western North Carolina (WNC), where LACE is endemic, is poorly known.METHODSWe administered an electronic survey to communicable disease nurses (CDNs), environmental health specialists (EHS), and health directors in 10 WNC health departments with the highest reported incidence of LACE. The survey evaluated mosquito-borne disease knowledge and surveillance and control capacity based on respondent public health roles.RESULTSResponses were received from all surveyed health departments. A total of 47 public health professionals (16 CDNs, 23 EHS, and 8 health directors) completed the survey, resulting in a 36.7% response rate. One (10%) department was rated as “fully capable” based on national mosquito surveillance and control standards. Respondents identified gaps in knowledge of case definitions, serology interpretation, environmental and behavioral risk factors, and vector control capacity. Although most participants recognized the importance of preventing and controlling mosquito-borne disease, assessments of response capabilities varied by respondent job role.LIMITATIONSThis study was limited by sample size, moderate response rate, timing of the assessment, and reliance on self-reported data. Variability in job roles may have influenced how questions were interpreted.CONCLUSIONSThis study serves as a foundational assessment of mosquito-borne disease control capacity among health departments in WNC, where LACE remains a public health concern. Our findings highlight the need for improved preparedness through education and resources, and the findings also support a regional approach to strengthen prevention, detection, and response efforts.Keywords: La Crosse, encephalitis, mosquito, surveillance, vector-borne disease, Michael Ratliff, Sarah Brill Thach, Amy Lanou, Carl Williams, Brian Byrd
full_text_sections.methods: MethodsThis study employed a cross-sectional survey to assess knowledge of vector-borne diseases and control capacity in 10 county-based health departments in WNC (Figure 1). These counties had the highest cumulative incidence of La Crosse encephalitis between 2000 and 2020.7 The primary data collection tool was an electronic survey developed using SurveyMonkey© software (San Mateo, CA). The survey contained 80 total items, including a combination of core questions administered to all participants and role-specific questions tailored to health directors, environmental health specialists, or communicable disease nurses. No individual respondent completed more than 32 questions. The full survey instrument is available from the corresponding author upon request.Figure 1.A) Map of the Study Area: Participating Western North Carolina Counties with the Highest Cumulative Incidence of Neuroinvasive La Crosse Virus Disease, 2000–2020; B) Respondents’ Ratings of Health Department Preparedness to Respond to Mosquito-Borne Disease CasesFigure note. Preparedness was assessed on a 7-point scale: 1 = extremely prepared and 7 = extremely unprepared. Respondents (N = 46) included local county health directors (HD, n = 8), communicable disease nurses (CDN, n = 16) and environmental health specialists (EHS, n = 22).A map of the state of turkey AI-generated content may be incorrect.The survey assessed vector-borne disease knowledge, perceptions of public health relevance, and existing mosquito surveillance and control capacity. Survey content assessing control capacity was structured around core and supplemental competencies recognized by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and adapted from the National Association of County and City Health Officials (NACCHO) framework for mosquito control programs.5 Because LACV is the most common mosquito-borne pathogen causing human disease in WNC, the scope of the survey was primarily focused on LACV and mosquito-borne disease response instead of other vector-borne diseases.The Office of Human Research Ethics at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill determined that this study did not meet the federal definition of human subjects research [45 CFR 46.102(e) or (l); 21 CFR 56.102(c), (e), or (l)] and therefore did not require Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval.Participants included health department directors, communicable disease nurses (CDNs), and registered environmental health specialists or interns (EHS). These specific job roles were selected as they have clearly defined roles as part of the public health response to “arboviral encephalitis/meningitis” as described in the local health department investigation steps within the North Carolina Communicable Disease Manual.22 Potential respondents were identified through a review of health department websites, the North Carolina State Board of Environmental Health Specialist Examiners registry, and professional contacts. The survey was distributed via email to 128 verified email addresses (10 health department directors, 18 CDNs, and 100 EHS). The survey remained open for 4 weeks (February 2024–March 2024), during which two reminder emails and follow-up phone calls were used to encourage participation.Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and contingency tables to compare vector-borne disease preparedness across roles. Basic data analyses (e.g., descriptive and summary statistics) were performed within the SurveyMonkey© website directly or exported to a .csv file for analyses using R/RStudio.23 Confidence intervals were calculated using the exact binomial method. Significance was defined a priori as P < .05 for all statistical tests. For paired ranking data, a global Friedman test was conducted first. When the Friedman test was statistically significant, pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were performed. Data visualizations and graphs were created using ggplot2 in R/RStudio.24
full_text_sections.results: ResultsResponse RatesThe survey was distributed via email to 128 public health staff across 10 WNC local health departments. Of these, 62 individuals initiated the survey, and 60 individuals acknowledged the consent statement and identified their professional role as either a health director, environmental health specialist (EHS), or communicable disease nurse (CDN). Within individual counties, the number of respondents initiating the survey ranged from 2 to 12, (median: 6; mean: 6.7). A total of 47 participants completed the survey in full, resulting in an overall response rate of 36.7%. Public health personnel from all 10 health departments completed the survey, including 8 health directors, 23 EHS personnel, and 16 CDNs (the CDNs include 2 respondents that identified as public health nurses with communicable disease reporting or investigation responsibilities). Overall survey completion rates for specific job roles varied (80% of health directors, 23% of EHS, and 84.2% of CDNs); because individuals were allowed to skip questions during the survey, the responses to any single question may not equal the total number of participants.Health Department Preparedness to Respond to Mosquito-Borne DiseasesRespondents ranked their health department’s level of preparedness to respond to mosquito-borne disease cases, where 1 = extremely prepared, 2 = very prepared, 3 = somewhat prepared, 4 = unsure, 5 = somewhat unprepared, 6 = very unprepared, and 7 = extremely unprepared. Overall (N = 46), the median response was 3 (somewhat prepared) (mean: 3.63; range 2–7) (Figure 1). Although health directors responded more favorably (median: 2.5; mean: 2.9; range 2–5) and EHS personnel responded less favorably (median: 4; mean: 4.3; range 2–7), these differences were not statistically significant.Perceived Relative Importance of Mosquito-Borne DiseasesRespondents ranked selected mosquito-borne diseases in order of importance (public health relevance) for their respective counties (Figure 2). The choices included the following endemic and travel-related mosquito-borne diseases: eastern equine encephalitis, chikungunya virus disease, La Crosse encephalitis, malaria, St. Louis encephalitis, West Nile encephalitis, and Zika virus disease; the default order choice in the survey was alphabetical. full_text_sections.discussion: DiscussionThis assessment clearly demonstrates that, despite recognizing La Crosse encephalitis (LACE) as the most important mosquito-borne disease in WNC, local health department personnel encounter challenges in preparedness, interpretation of diagnostic laboratory results, and resource availability. These findings underscore an urgent need for targeted investments in workforce training, surveillance infrastructure, and sustainable funding to support effective vector-borne disease response broadly. Surveillance and control capacities were notably limited across the region, and only one county met all 5 NACCHO-defined core and supplemental standards. Key capacities such as routine entomologic surveillance were reported by only a few health departments (Table 1). Knowledge of LACE-specific risk factors also varied, although CDN personnel generally demonstrated a stronger understanding of environmental and behavioral risk factors than EHS personnel; however, both groups exhibited gaps in identifying key behavioral risk factors and protective environmental factors. Most CDN respondents demonstrated difficulty accurately identifying La Crosse virus (LACV) as the likely cause of a case study (Appendix A), while 14.3% selected the correct agent despite appropriate clinical and laboratory evidence. The most common response (“the child’s disease was most likely caused by California encephalitis virus”) may demonstrate uncertainty about the members of the California serogroup of viruses. Additionally, 53.3% of CDN respondents recognized that the case met the laboratory criteria for an arboviral disease, indicating potential gaps in diagnostic interpretation.Our assessment also revealed meaningful barriers to improving local vector-borne disease response. Most health directors cited limited personnel capacity as the primary constraint, emphasizing the need for sustained funding to support capacity building. State and federal financial support was rare, and health departments reported limited awareness of existing external resources. The one county that had all 5 core and supplemental mosquito control and surveillance capabilities was also the only county reporting active state funding (AA908 contracts). While most EHS respondents recognized vector-borne disease prevention as a professional responsibility and expressed interest in participating, many felt unqualified or too overburdened to provide such services. Overall, the health department personnel expressed strong interest in increased training opportunities. Respondents favored short (1-day) regional offerings focused on practical skills such as mosquito identification, laboratory result interpretation, and disease trends. These findings highlight a regional need for increased investment in personnel, training, and infrastructure to strengthen preparedness and response capacity for LACV and other mosquito-borne pathogens.LimitationsThis study was limited by a small sample size (N = 47), a moderate response rate (36.7%), and reliance on self-reported data. Variation in job roles may have affected how questions were interpreted. However, participation from all 10 WNC counties with the highest incidence of LACE disease and statistically significant findings for key risk factors and roles support the study’s robustness. Also, the low number of health directors (n = 8) limits the robustness of the study statistically, and thus their role-specific responses should be contextualized as such.The primary goal of this study was to evaluate LACV prevention, detection, and response capacity in North Carolina county health departments. Other public health agencies, namely the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Public Health & Human Services agency and the North Carolina Public Health Preparedness and Response branch (North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services) were not included in this survey. Future efforts to develop a regional approach to LACV prevention, detection, and response should include these important partners. The survey was developed using CDC and NACCHO vector control capacity guidance with additional questions developed by state and regional vector-borne disease subject matter experts. The instrument was designed as an applied public health capacity assessment rather than a psychometric scale. As such, formal scale validation methods were not conducted. The survey included both role-specific response items and structural indicators to evaluate operational realities across health departments.This study was conducted in 2024, nearly a year after the World Health Organization announced the end of the COVID-19 epidemic as a public health emergency of international concern.27 The impacts of COVID-19 on the public and environmental health workforce clearly limited vector-borne disease preparedness and response, as many personnel had to shift priorities to support the pandemic response. These shifts contributed to underdiagnosis, underreporting, and reduced data availability in 2020 and 2021, which likely continues to affect funding, staffing, and institutional prioritization of vector-borne diseases in local health departments.28 The results of our study should thus be contextualized with the potential lingering impacts of COVID-19 in addition to other shifting public health priorities and chronic public health workforce challenges.3 Furthermore, the survey was conducted in February and March of 2024, which is outside the typical time when mosquito activity is common in WNC. Finally, while the assessment presented here emphasizes LACV, the survey instrument assessed vector-borne disease capacity more broadly, and respondents may have interpreted some items in the context of general mosquito-borne disease preparedness rather than LACV specifically.ConclusionGoing forward, the information gained from our survey can be used to prioritize training interventions to improve LACE case prevention, detection, and response capacity for WNC. Training sessions, including the use of case studies, to help improve CDN knowledge and application of case definitions for La Crosse encephalitis (and other vector-borne diseases) should be developed. Given that LACE is clearly recognized as a regional public health issue and that individual counties report very few cases each year, it may be more effective to use a regional approach to training and vector control that combines personnel, equipment, and other resources for case investigations and response. By leveraging coordinated approaches like region-specific training opportunities (e.g., tabletop exercises simulating local mosquito-borne disease outbreaks; mosquito surveillance and control workshops; virtual competency-based trainings for arboviral laboratory test interpretation), WNC can more effectively build the workforce capacity, surveillance systems, and resource-sharing networks needed to reduce the burden of LACE and other vector-borne diseases.Disclosure of InterestsThe authors have no relevant conflicts of interest relating to this study.CorrespondenceAddress correspondence to Dr. Brian Byrd, Western Carolina University, 3971 Little Savannah Road, Cullowhee, NC 28723 (bdbyrd@wcu.edu).

full_text_sections.other: IntroductionIn recent decades, vector-borne infectious disease incidence has tripled in the United States.1,2 Despite this increase, many regions across the United States lack adequate public health infrastructure, mosquito surveillance and control capacity, and invasive vector detection capabilities.3–5 In North Carolina, the primary causes of endemic mosquito-borne disease are La Crosse, eastern equine encephalitis (EEE), and West Nile viruses. In most years, La Crosse encephalitis (LACE) accounts for the largest burden of endemic mosquito-borne disease in the state.6,7 Notably, LACE disproportionately impacts children, with a median case age of 9 years.7 During the past two decades, persistent spatial clusters of LACE have been identified in Western North Carolina (WNC) counties.8La Crosse virus (LACV) is an arbovirus in the genus Orthobunyavirus and a member of California serogroup (CSG) of viruses. The CSG contains 18 viruses, including species such as Jamestown Canyon virus that overlaps geographically and is antigenically similar, resulting in cross-reactivity for some diagnostic methods.9,10 The disease ecology of LACV is complex. The virus is primarily transmitted by the eastern tree hole mosquito (Aedes triseriatus), although two invasive mosquito species (Aedes albopictus and Aedes japonicus) are likely secondary vectors.11 Horizontal transmission includes virus-amplifying hosts such as chipmunks and squirrels (family Sciuridae).12 Humans are “dead end” hosts as they do not appear to have detectable viremias that are able to infect host-feeding mosquitoes. Importantly, LACV can be vertically transmitted from a female mosquito to her offspring via transovarial infection, which likely leads to the spatial persistence of the virus over decades.13,14From a national perspective, LACE is rare.2 However, in areas of Appalachia where the disease is endemic, the relative risk of disease in high-risk clusters can be 23 to 70 times higher than non-endemic counties.15 From 2003–2021, the risk of LACE was approximately 44 to 53 times higher in WNC high-risk clusters than in non-endemic counties, clearly demonstrating the regional importance of this disease. papers.title_original: Vector-Borne Disease Preparedness in Western North Carolina: Assessing Health Department Capacity for La Crosse Encephalitis Prevention and Response

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to assess the capacity of health departments in Western North Carolina to prevent and respond to mosquito-borne diseases, with a focus on La Crosse encephalitis (LACE) as the leading cause of pediatric arboviral encephalitis in the United States.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among communicable disease nurses (CDNs), environmental health specialists (EHS), and health directors in 10 WNC health departments with the highest reported incidence of LACE. A total of 47 public health professionals completed the survey, resulting in a 36.7% response rate.
analysis.methods: The study employed an electronic survey to assess knowledge of vector-borne diseases and control capacity. Preparedness was evaluated using a 7-point scale, and significance was defined a priori as P < .05 for all statistical tests.
analysis.main_results: One department was rated as fully capable based on national mosquito surveillance and control standards. LACE was ranked as the most important mosquito-borne disease of public health relevance by respondents. EHS personnel were more accurate than CDN personnel in identifying that the presence of a creek or pond near a residence are not LACE risk factors.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that while most participants recognized the importance of preventing mosquito-borne diseases, there was variation in their assessment of response capabilities. The study highlights the need for improved preparedness through education and resources.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results inform the need for targeted education and resource allocation to enhance mosquito-borne disease preparedness, particularly for LACE, and support the development of a regional approach to strengthen prevention and response efforts.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study was limited by a moderate response rate, small sample size for health directors, timing of the assessment, and reliance on self-reported data. The evidence strength is moderate due to these limitations.

analysis.summary_en: This study assessed the capacity of 10 Western North Carolina health departments to prevent and respond to mosquito-borne diseases, with a focus on La Crosse encephalitis (LACE). A cross-sectional survey was administered to communicable disease nurses, environmental health specialists, and health directors, resulting in a 36.7% response rate. Most participants recognized the importance of mosquito-borne disease prevention, but assessments of response capabilities varied by job role. LACE was ranked as the most important disease of public health relevance, and EHS personnel were more accurate than CDN personnel in identifying risk factors. The study highlights the need for improved preparedness through education and resources, but its findings are limited by a moderate response rate, small sample size for health directors, and reliance on self-reported data. The evidence strength is moderate, as the study provides insights into health department capacities but lacks comprehensive data.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 这项研究旨在评估北卡罗来纳州西部卫生部门预防和应对蚊媒疾病的能力,重点关注拉克罗斯脑炎(LACE),它是美国小儿虫媒病毒脑炎的主要原因。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 对 LACE 报告 发病率 最高的 10 个 WNC 卫生部门的传染病护士 (CDN)、环境卫生专家 (EHS) 和卫生主管进行了一项横断面调查。共有 47 名公共卫生专业人员完成了调查,回复率为 36.7%。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究采用电子调查来评估对 媒介 传播疾病的了解和控制能力。使用 7 级量表评估准备情况,所有统计检验的显着性均被先验定义为 P < .05。
elements_zh.main_results: 1个部门根据国家灭蚊监测和防治标准被评为完全能力。受访者将 LACE 列为与公共卫生相关的最重要的蚊媒疾病。EHS 人员比 CDN 人员更准确地识别出住宅附近存在的小溪或池塘不是 LACE 风险因素。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果表明,虽然大多数参与者认识到预防蚊媒疾病的重要性,但他们对应对能力的评估存在差异。该研究强调需要通过教育和资源改善准备工作。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 结果表明需要进行有针对性的教育和资源分配,以加强蚊媒疾病的防范,特别是针对 LACE,并支持制定区域方法以加强预防和应对工作。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究受到反应率适中、卫生主管样本量小、评估时间安排以及对自我报告数据依赖的限制。由于这些限制,证据强度中等。

papers.title: Interdisciplinary human-centric architectural framework for One Health surveillance, early warning, and response: leveraging AI modelling and IoT environmental monitoring

source_records.title: Interdisciplinary human-centric architectural framework for One Health surveillance, early warning, and response: leveraging AI modelling and IoT environmental monitoring
Interdisciplinary human-centric architectural framework for One Health surveillance, early warning, and response: leveraging AI modelling and IoT environmental monitoring

papers.full_text: AbstractSuccessful pandemic preparedness and sustainable healthcare security increasingly rely on One Health—linking humans, animals, and the environment. Novel real-time geolocated data sources from social media, the web, digital traces, and Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, combined with traditional surveillance data, are increasingly used to power AI models and enhance environmental sensing that is essential for preparedness and response in the One Health context. Despite the abundance of data streams and sensing data, the potential of AI and IoT environmental monitoring for One Health remains unfulfilled. The OHSEW (One Health Surveillance and Early Warning) framework architecture fills this gap by defining a human-centric architecture for One Health surveillance, early warning, and response, leveraging AI modelling and IoT environmental sensing, designed in particular for monitoring vector-borne diseases, zoonoses, and other environmental reservoirs of infectious diseases where the risk of spillover to human populations is high. In the OHSEW framework, we identify a rich spectrum of multiple heterogeneous data sources and a pipeline for improved surveillance, data visualisation, and training predictive AI models. These include open-source population and socioeconomic data, land use, satellite sensing, and weather forecasts, enriched by IoT environmental sensing (providing microclimate data streams) and traditional routine surveillance data reported by public health and environmental health experts. These models generate real-time data and actionable evidence for public health managers and policymakers, visualised through customisable dashboards, and provide early warning signals enabling rapid response and effective risk communication with the public. In this article, we outline the framework architecture, individual components, data pipeline, and configurable and localisable setup. To demonstrate the feasibility of the architecture, components of the OHSEW framework were piloted in real-world deployments of mosquito surveillance systems at two sites, Madeira, Portugal, and Cabedelo, Brazil. The architectures and results of these real-world deployments are presented to illustrate the feasibility of the OHSEW framework, with directions for further research outlined.Keywords: AI modelling, architecture framework, Internet of Things, One Health, vector-borne disease 4.Discussion and Future WorkIn this section, we will discuss the strengths of the framework to consider when implementing OHSEW, the key challenges to address, and opportunities for scale-up.4.1.StrengthsThe main strengths are interdisciplinarity, privacy, transparency, data standardisation and interoperability, and generalisability. Interdisciplinary The architecture will be driven by and used by public health and One Health experts, while the details of analysis, bias, and AI model training will be led by public health experts and ecologists rather than AI engineers. Through the process of adoption and localisation of the framework for their specific needs, users might prefer to tune the architecture for impact and environmental plausibility or opt for simple yet tailored solutions rather than fully generic ones with the best precision and recall. Privacy Data privacy and responsible data sharing are recommended to be built into the system and protected through open data frameworks, as defined in Layer 2, rather than treated as an afterthought (63). This is an essential matter of public trust in technology, which was severely dented after COVID-19 with the arrival of Big Tech in healthcare and governments (64). Data standardisation and interoperability Well-defined standards need to be defined and implemented in Layers 1 and 2: One Health Data and Data Integration through a Federated Architecture. Generalisability While the pilot was implemented for mosquito-borne disease surveillance, the framework and associated tools are generalisable to routine data collection for other vectors—we are currently exploring the adaptation of the digital tools for tick surveillance.Engagement with public health stakeholders builds on the collaboration from the mosquito surveillance networks. Implementing OHSEW for human disease surveillance, such as influenza or influenza-like illness (ILI), will require engagement of public health agencies, access to and sharing of reported data, and use of data provided by participatory surveillance apps such as InfluenzaNet2 (popular due to the high prevalence of the disease in the community, which was not the case for VBDs). However, the components and pipeline of the OHSEW framework will remain the same.4.2.Challenges and LimitationsIn this section, we outline key challenges to address when building AI predictive systems using the OHSEW framework, aligned with generic principles of responsible AI (39). While a detailed discussion of these principles is beyond the scope of this study, we outline a suitable governance framework and key studies to follow. Explainability AI-generated models used in the framework cannot be non-reproducible black boxes (65); they need to be sufficiently transparent and interpretable to be trusted to support scientific learning and decision-making (42). Surveillance ethics and data abuse Ethical challenges for AI in public health surveillance have been well understood (39). These include concerns over the access to and use of citizens’ private data, such as phone mobility data (e.g., COVID-19 proximity tracking), due to the danger of disproportionate surveillance, policy measures for enforcement of compliance, unfair false positives, and documented data misuse (39, 66). However, data ownership and data access in public health (67) are societal challenges that we are currently grappling with, rather than being exclusive to One Health (68). Noise and misinformation Noise from digital data sources, fake accounts, and trolls on social media can exacerbate misinformation, making the extraction of meaningful information increasingly challenging (69). Prudence with incorporating social media (especially X) is recommended. Methods for filtering low-quality, biased news and misinformation are also recommended, as shown by an analysis of Twitter during COVID-19 (70) and around HPV vaccine misinformation (71, 72). These studies demonstrated that misinformation often originates from a small number of accounts and sources. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractSuccessful pandemic preparedness and sustainable healthcare security increasingly rely on One Health—linking humans, animals, and the environment. Novel real-time geolocated data sources from social media, the web, digital traces, and Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, combined with traditional surveillance data, are increasingly used to power AI models and enhance environmental sensing that is essential for preparedness and response in the One Health context. Despite the abundance of data streams and sensing data, the potential of AI and IoT environmental monitoring for One Health remains unfulfilled. The OHSEW (One Health Surveillance and Early Warning) framework architecture fills this gap by defining a human-centric architecture for One Health surveillance, early warning, and response, leveraging AI modelling and IoT environmental sensing, designed in particular for monitoring vector-borne diseases, zoonoses, and other environmental reservoirs of infectious diseases where the risk of spillover to human populations is high. In the OHSEW framework, we identify a rich spectrum of multiple heterogeneous data sources and a pipeline for improved surveillance, data visualisation, and training predictive AI models. These include open-source population and socioeconomic data, land use, satellite sensing, and weather forecasts, enriched by IoT environmental sensing (providing microclimate data streams) and traditional routine surveillance data reported by public health and environmental health experts. These models generate real-time data and actionable evidence for public health managers and policymakers, visualised through customisable dashboards, and provide early warning signals enabling rapid response and effective risk communication with the public. In this article, we outline the framework architecture, individual components, data pipeline, and configurable and localisable setup. To demonstrate the feasibility of the architecture, components of the OHSEW framework were piloted in real-world deployments of mosquito surveillance systems at two sites, Madeira, Portugal, and Cabedelo, Brazil. The architectures and results of these real-world deployments are presented to illustrate the feasibility of the OHSEW framework, with directions for further research outlined.Keywords: AI modelling, architecture framework, Internet of Things, One Health, vector-borne disease

papers.title_original: Interdisciplinary human-centric architectural framework for One Health surveillance, early warning, and response: leveraging AI modelling and IoT environmental monitoring

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to develop an interdisciplinary human-centric architectural framework for One Health surveillance, early warning, and response, leveraging AI modelling and IoT environmental monitoring to address the challenges of emerging infectious diseases, particularly those originating from animals, which pose significant threats to public health.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved a real-world pilot deployment of the OHSEW framework for mosquito-borne disease surveillance in Brazil and Madeira over a 2-year period, focusing on the feasibility of integrating diverse data sources for disease monitoring and response.
analysis.methods: The methods included the development of an AI-driven framework that integrates real-time geolocated data from social media, the web, digital traces, and IoT sensors with traditional surveillance data, while also addressing challenges in filtering low-quality, biased news and misinformation.
analysis.main_results: The framework was demonstrated to be feasible through a pilot deployment for mosquito surveillance, which showed the potential of combining AI and IoT data for early warning. Additionally, the study highlighted the increasing role of AI models in analyzing genomic data from humans, animals, and environmental sources for early detection of diseases like chikungunya.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted the results as demonstrating the potential of the OHSEW framework to enhance surveillance and response capabilities, particularly for diseases with animal origins. The novelty lies in the integration of AI and IoT technologies with traditional surveillance data to create a more comprehensive and responsive system.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that the OHSEW framework can improve the detection and response to emerging infectious diseases, including chikungunya, by leveraging interdisciplinary data sources and AI technologies. This has important implications for enhancing global surveillance and preparedness.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study acknowledges limitations in the generalisability of the framework, as it was primarily tested for mosquito-borne diseases. However, the evidence is considered moderate due to the pilot nature of the implementation and the need for further research to validate its effectiveness across different contexts.

analysis.summary_en: This study presents an interdisciplinary human-centric architectural framework for One Health surveillance, early warning, and response, leveraging AI modelling and IoT environmental monitoring. The framework integrates real-time geolocated data from social media, the web, digital traces, and IoT sensors with traditional surveillance data to enhance environmental sensing and preparedness. A pilot deployment for mosquito-borne disease surveillance in Brazil and Madeira over two years demonstrated the feasibility of the OHSEW framework. The study highlights the increasing use of AI models in analyzing genomic data from humans, animals, and environmental sources for early warning. The authors interpret these results as showing the potential of the framework to improve surveillance and response to diseases with animal origins, such as chikungunya. The findings suggest that the OHSEW framework can enhance global surveillance and preparedness for emerging infectious diseases. However, the study notes limitations in generalisability, as the framework was primarily tested for mosquito-borne diseases, and further research is needed to validate its effectiveness across different contexts.

papers.title: Arboviroses no município de Limoeiro: análise dos registros entre 2021 e 2025 e ação educativa no ensino médio
papers.abstract: As arboviroses constituem um importante problema de saúde pública e sua abordagem no ambiente escolar pode contribuir para a compreensão das formas de transmissão e prevenção. Este estudo teve como objetivo analisar os registros de dengue, chikungunya e zika no município de Limoeiro, Pernambuco, entre 2021 e 2025, e descrever uma ação educativa realizada com estudantes do ensino médio. Desenvolveu-se um estudo descritivo, de abordagem quantitativa, organizado em duas etapas complementares. Na primeira, foram analisados dados secundários fornecidos pela Secretaria Municipal de Saúde de Limoeiro e consultados no DATASUS, mediante o cálculo de frequências absolutas e relativas. Na segunda, realizou-se uma intervenção com uma turma do 1o ano da Escola de Referência em Ensino Médio Dr. Sebastião de Vasconcelos Galvão, composta por uma palestra dialogada e pelo jogo ‘Bingo temático: arboviroses’. No período analisado, foram contabilizados 4.784 registros: 4.203 de dengue (87,9%), 471 de chikungunya (9,8%) e 110 de zika (2,3%). A dengue predominou em todos os anos e alcançou 1.621 registros em 2025. Durante a ação educativa, observaram-se participação, interação e cooperação entre os estudantes. Conclui-se que a utilização de informações epidemiológicas locais, associada a uma atividade lúdica, pode aproximar os conteúdos científicos da realidade escolar e favorecer o diálogo sobre prevenção. Entretanto, a ausência de avaliação sistemática limita as conclusões sobre os efeitos da intervenção na aprendizagem.
authors: Rita de Cássia Freire de Melo Goldbaum
papers.journal: Revista edUCA - Revista Multidisciplinar da Faculdade Católica Paulista

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to analyze the records of dengue, chikungunya, and Zika in Limoeiro, Pernambuco, between 2021 and 2025, and describe an educational intervention with high school students. It employed a descriptive quantitative approach, divided into two complementary stages: one involving secondary data analysis from the municipal health department and DATASUS, and the other involving an educational activity with a class of first-year students. The results showed that dengue was the most prevalent, accounting for 87.9% of the 4,784 total records, with 1,621 cases in 2025. Chikungunya and Zika accounted for 9.8% and 2.3%, respectively. The educational intervention was observed to promote student participation, interaction, and cooperation. The authors concluded that integrating local epidemiological data with interactive activities can bring scientific content closer to the school context and encourage dialogue on prevention. However, the lack of systematic evaluation limits the conclusions about the intervention's impact on learning. The study provides insights into the epidemiological patterns of arboviruses and highlights the potential of educational strategies in public health.

papers.title_zh: 利莫埃罗市的树病毒:2021 年和 2025 年的登记分析以及媒介教育
papers.source_body_en: As arboviroses constituem um importante problema de saúde pública e sua abordagem no ambiente escolar pode contribuir para a compreensão das formas de transmissão e prevenção. Este estudo teve como objetivo analisar os registros de dengue, chikungunya e zika no município de Limoeiro, Pernambuco, entre 2021 e 2025, e descrever uma ação educativa realizada com estudantes do ensino médio. Desenvolveu-se um estudo descritivo, de abordagem quantitativa, organizado em duas etapas complementares. Na primeira, foram analisados dados secundários fornecidos pela Secretaria Municipal de Saúde de Limoeiro e consultados no DATASUS, mediante o cálculo de frequências absolutas e relativas. Na segunda, realizou-se uma intervenção com uma turma do 1o ano da Escola de Referência em Ensino Médio Dr. Sebastião de Vasconcelos Galvão, composta por uma palestra dialogada e pelo jogo ‘Bingo temático: arboviroses’. No período analisado, foram contabilizados 4.784 registros: 4.203 de dengue (87,9%), 471 de chikungunya (9,8%) e 110 de zika (2,3%). A dengue predominou em todos os anos e alcançou 1.621 registros em 2025. Durante a ação educativa, observaram-se participação, interação e cooperação entre os estudantes. Conclui-se que a utilização de informações epidemiológicas locais, associada a uma atividade lúdica, pode aproximar os conteúdos científicos da realidade escolar e favorecer o diálogo sobre prevenção. Entretanto, a ausência de avaliação sistemática limita as conclusões sobre os efeitos da intervenção na aprendizagem.

source_records.title: Syndirella: synthesis-directed fragment elaboration enables extensive and cost-effective binding site exploration beyond catalog compounds

papers.full_text: AbstractFragment screens provide an information-rich starting point for designing derivative compounds in structure-based drug discovery. However, derivatives in the fragment-to-hit stage are typically designed from only one or a few fragments, risking premature convergence on an unproductive series and dramatically limiting exploration of the binding site's interaction opportunities. This is avoidable by exploring a broad, chemically diverse set of scaffolds and elaborations spanning interactions revealed across many fragments, as well as those not yet observed. Conventional catalog procurement makes this breadth of testing prohibitively expensive for early discovery. In-house high-throughput (HT) synthesis can raise interaction productivity, the number of unique predicted protein–ligand interactions achievable within a given budget, by lowering the cost per compound, including labor and consumables, yet no design tool exists for this purpose. We introduce Syndirella (Synthesis Directed Elaborations), which presents a candidate elaboration space around input fragment-derived scaffolds, constrained to HT-compatible reactions and catalog reactants, for cost-effective sampling of many scaffolds' elaborations in a single experimental cycle. Applied to three viral protein targets, Syndirella designs demonstrated pharmacophore diversity, recapitulating known fragment interactions, identifying novel functionally relevant ones, and accessing chemical space absent from commercial catalogs. A companion paper details validation on a calcium-binding protein, yielding crystallographic structures and measurable binding, with in-house synthesis achieving a 71% cost reduction over catalog purchasing, labor and consumables included. Reactant rather than product procurement gives potentially 2.5 times as many accessible compounds and higher interaction productivity for the same budget. Syndirella is most impactful for structure-enabled campaigns with fragment-bound crystal structures, robust HT chemistry, and assays compatible with crude reaction mixtures, and is available at https://github.com/oxpig/syndirella. Syndirella proposes elaborations of fragment-derived scaffolds for high-throughput synthesis using in-catalog reactants for SAR exploration. MethodsSyndirella takes as input fragment or fragment-derived scaffold structures and outputs congeneric series with 3D poses and associated synthetic routes suitable for HT synthesis. For each scaffold, synthetic routes are first solved using a retrosynthesis tool or defined manually, and for each required reactant, a superstructure search is performed under constraints that preserve the reaction site. The resulting reactant superstructures are combined to yield a large set of elaborated products, which are then energy-minimized in silico into the experimental protein structure with strong constraints to the experimental fragment pose using Fragmenstein.51 Predicted conformations are subsequently scored and filtered based on geometry checks and modeled binding energy. The pipeline is tunable and expandable to accommodate the specific capabilities and preferences of downstream HT synthesis experiments.Computational workflowSyndirella produces congeneric series of compounds from input scaffolds with fragment origin. These scaffolds can be fragments themselves or derivatives from fragment growing, linking, or most commonly in this work, fragment merges.52 Fragment merged compounds can be proposed algorithmically or manually, although design methods should prioritize the recapitulation of fragment atoms. One algorithmic method that implements fragment merging and is extensively used throughout our pipeline is Fragmenstein.51 Fragmenstein combines atoms from fragments using structural information to create derivatives that are predicted to adopt the same binding pose as the fragments. Additionally, Wills et al. utilized the Fragment Network,53,54 first described by Astex Pharmaceuticals,15 where traversing a graph database of compounds starting from a fragment node leads to derivative compounds that recapitulate fragment–protein interactions. Compounds that are used as input into the complete Syndirella workflow are hereafter referred to as scaffolds, shown in Fig. 1.Fig. 1Workflow of Syndirella starting from a fragment-inspired scaffold, the pipeline defines synthetic routes, identifies superstructures of reactants from chemical catalogs, predicts products via combinatorial synthesis, and performs placement relative to inspiration fragments using Fragmenstein.51 The example shows a two-step synthesis (amidation and Suzuki coupling) where final products (thick representation) are overlaid with original fragments (thin representation), with successful placements indicated by green checkmarks and not successful by red crosses.Pose generation of scaffolds and filteringFirst, poses are generated for input scaffolds to filter out those which do not have an energetically favorable conformation in the binding site. Pose generation is performed using the tool Fragmenstein,51 although any pose generation method could be used, whether restrained to the parent fragment pose or not. Fragmenstein generates an initial pose by calculating the positional overlap between the compound and fragments used for the original merge. The atoms on the compound found in this overlap are restricted to the coordinates from the fragments. This unphysical conformation undergoes energy minimization placed in the apo protein template specified by the user. Energy minimization is controlled by either PyRosetta's scorefunction ref2015 (ref. 55) or RDKit's UFF.56 For the analysis shown here, minimization with RDKit's UFF was performed unless specified otherwise. When using PyRosetta, the sidechains of protein residues with alpha carbons within 8 Å of the centroid of the compound are energy minimized whereas the protein is fixed when performing UFF minimization. A ΔΔG score is calculated by Fragmenstein as a single snapshot difference of the final bound state minus the unbound state (see ref. 51). It should be mentioned that this ΔΔG score should not be interpreted as a robust free binding energy and instead is used only as a filter where if the score is ≥0 the pose is most likely energetically unfavorable and strained.Scaffolds that complete energy minimization within 240 s, have an RMSD of <2 Å to the inspiration fragments, have a ΔΔG score of <0, and pass PoseBuster's intramolecular geometry checks for bond lengths, angles, steric clashes, and aromatic ring planarity are accepted.57Route modeling for HT synthesisFor each scaffold that passes pose generation, Syndirella proposes elaborations by explicit SMIRKS-encoded forward synthesis route modelling with any number of reaction steps.58 First, route selection is specified for the scaffold manually or proposed by a retrosynthesis tool. Here in this analysis using Manifold (https://postera.ai/), although functionality using the open-source tool AiZynthFinder is also provided. When using Manifold, the catalogs specified to query were enamine_bb, mcule, mcule_ultimate, enamine_real, enamine_made, and generic (common molecules that are found in most catalogs).59–61 For a compound to be considered “elaboratable”, there must be a forward synthesis route with all reactions encoded in Syndirella's SMIRKS library. Syndirella includes 109 SMIRKS encoded reactions which have been specifically chosen for HT chemistry. In this work 23 were used (available as RXN_SMIRKS_CONSTANTS.json on Zenodo62) and since this analysis, more have been added with a significant amount from Dobbelaere et al.63 and are found at https://github.com/oxpig/syndirella.Syndirella prioritizes user synthesis preferencesSyndirella's reaction repertoire can be expanded or edited by adding a SMIRKS pattern58 representing the reaction of interest (e.g., sourced from resources such as SMARTS-RX64 or SmartReact65). Additionally, reaction substitutions can be specified to suit user preferences based on better yield history or usually cheaper reactants. For example, replacing Schotten–Baumann reactions with amidations often improves building block availability and reduces cost (Fig. S4). Each alternative reaction generates an additional and separate synthesis route and can be specified in a .json format and example jupyter notebooks to generate these files are provided (see https://github.com/oxpig/syndirella).Superstructure search of reactants to produce elaborated productsTo produce the series, each reactant in the forward synthesis route is elaborated and the full Cartesian product of the reactants is computed in silico. The following steps are taken for each reaction step in the forward synthesis route. First, the original reactants are labeled with the specific reactant number in the SMIRKS of that reaction. Then, each reactant is used as a query in a superstructure search – performed by Manifold in this work, although functionality using the catalog search tool Arthor (https://arthor.docking.org/) is provided. A superstructure of a query compound is a compound that contains the query compound as a maximum common substructure. In this analysis, the catalogs queried were enamine_bb, mcule, mcule_ultimate, enamine_real, enamine_made, and generic (common molecules that are found in most catalogs).59–61Superstructure reactants are filtered by removing duplicates, compounds containing non-abundant isotopes, compounds that don't match the reactant SMIRKS, and if the number of atom difference to the query reactant is <0 or >10 (although these thresholds can be changed to user preferences). If the step is a bimolecular reaction, reactants that contain both reacting groups are excluded to reduce selectivity issues.Product compounds are generated from the full Cartesian product of the smallest 100 reactants for bimolecular reactions or by the smallest 10 K reactants for unimolecular reactions, thereby restricting the total number of products in each step to ≤10 K (although this threshold can be changed to user preferences). For each reactant combination, the product is determined by the original SMIRKS reaction pattern. Products are excluded if they cannot be sanitized by the RDKit.66 If multiple products are produced for a single combination, the product is flagged with a selectivity issue label.The previous steps repeat for each reaction step until the final products are determined and labeled with their InChi key and ordered in ascending atom count. All stereoisomers are enumerated and the SMILES and full routes are stored as a dataframe.67,68Pose generation of products and filteringEach compound must be placed into the protein pocket to predict the interactions between the compound and residues. The smallest 10 K elaborations after stereo enumeration are placed and filtered following the same steps detailed above for scaffold placement, although this threshold can be changed to user preferences.XChem data setsThe three test cases used in this work are publicly available crystallographic fragment screens from the XChem facility,69,70 summarized in Table 1 and are available for download from the Fragalysis platform (https://fragalysis.diamond.ac.uk). Scaffolds from these datasets were derived from three sources: computational fragment merging algorithms (either Knitwork53,54 or Fragmenstein51), exact fragment hits, or manually designed fragment merges.Table 1Summary of scaffolds used as test dataTargetOriginCountUnique fragment combinationsChikungunya virus nsP3 macrodomain (CHIKV-Mac)Fragmenstein317616Manual14 Total 331 Coxsackievirus A16 2A protease (EV-A71-2A)Exact348Knitwork42Manual76 Total 121 Enterovirus D68 3C protease (EV-D68-3C-PROA)Knitwork29158 Total 291 The Chikungunya virus nsP3 macrodomain protein (CHIKV-Mac) performs removal of ADP-ribose modifications to host proteins, an essential part of the replication process for Chikungunya virus.71 It has been shown mutants affecting ADP–ribose binding slows viral replication in mammalian cells and reduces virulence.72 A fragment screen was performed, resulting in 66 fragments bound in the ADP–ribose binding site and 616 unique combinations were used to design scaffolds by Fragmenstein and Knitwork.73Enterovirus A71 is a common cause of respiratory disease and hand, foot, and mouth disease in children worldwide.74 The 2A protease (EV-A71-2A) is responsible for a single intramolecular cleavage in the viral polyprotein, therefore targeting the active site could inhibit viral growth. Following a fragment screen on Coxsackievirus A16 2A protease which serves as a proxy for the highly conserved EV-A71-2A protein, 43 fragments were resolved in the active site and a variety of follow-up methods were utilized including manual designs to result in 121 scaffolds.75Similar to enterovirus A71, enterovirus D68 results in respiratory illness and in severe cases, paralysis.76 The 3C protease (EV-D68-3C) is required to cleave the non-structural part of the viral polyprotein. EV-D68-3C also cleaves many host proteins to facilitate viral infection thus, inhibition can reduce the viral replication by this target. The fragment screen of this target resulted in 16 fragments resolved in the active site, and only the Knitwork tool was used to propose 291 scaffolds.77All scaffolds input into the pipeline totaled to 743, hereafter referred to as the original-743. After inputting into Syndirella, successful series were defined as having >3 unique products and >0 successful placements of elaborations, totaling to 234, hereafter referred to as the successful-234 (Fig. S1).Cheminformatic analysisMorgan fingerprints with a radius of three and bit length of 2048 were used for all fingerprinting calculations using the RDKit.66,78 For the per cluster analysis, the mean Tanimoto values were calculated by taking the row-wise mean across the full Tanimoto similarity matrix for each elaboration in the cluster against all other molecules. Histograms of the mean Tanimoto values per cluster and smoothed by kernel density estimation using Seaborn's default parameters were calculated.79 All displays of chemical space by two dimensions were carried out by calculating the 50 first components from principal component decomposition of the Morgan fingerprints then transforming those components using the t-SNE algorithm. These transformations were carried out using the default parameters in scikit-learn.80R-group decomposition was carried out with the RDKit's RGroupDecompose function where the cores required to identify the R positions were the input scaffolds used.66 Then the R groups were filtered by removing repeats across all R positions and those with more than one attachment point. R-group pharmacophores were assigned per atom using the RDKit66 using the following custom rules. Hydrophobic, carbon with no N/O/S neighbour. Hydrogen bond donor (HBD), N or O bearing ≥1 hydrogen. Hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA), N or O bearing no hydrogen, or a neutral NH. Halogen, F/Cl/Br/I. Classes are non-exclusive. Each R group was summarized by the shortest topological (bond count) distance from the attachment point at which each class occurred, giving one pharmacophore-distance pair per class per R group.For the missing chemistry analysis, the original-743 were queried by Postera's Manifold for the top five retrosynthesis routes ordered by Manifold using the same catalogues as in Syndirella's default pipeline specifications.Comparison to traditional superstructure methodsThe scaffolds used as input for Arthor (https://arthor.docking.org/) and Manifold superstructure querying were a subset of the original-743 that passed placement filtered by the same constraints as described in the Computational workflow filtering section, resulting in 660 scaffolds, hereafter referred to as the scaffold-pass-660 (Fig. S1). For carrying out the Arthor queries, we queried the following databases: REAL-Database-22Q1, Mcule-22Q1-8.7M, Mcule-BB-22Q1-2.1M, Mcule-Full-22Q1-60M, Mcule-V-22Q1-51M, mcule_purchasable_virtual_230121, and Mcule-Ultimate-20Q2-126M. To reduce artificial attrition, a maximum of 10 K results per database query were analyzed (compared to 100 from the usual workflow). For the Manifold queries, we queried the following databases: enamine_bb, mcule, mcule_ultimate, enamine_real, enamine_made, and generic (common molecules that are found in most catalogs). For each database, a 900-page limit was applied to avoid unnecessary truncation (compared to 10 from the usual workflow). The compounds produced by Syndirella that were included in this analysis were all elaborations before filtering by placement. Compounds from all methods were compared by InChI key of the SMILES with all stereoisomer information removed.81The databases queried were matched as closely as possible across all methods to Syndirella's default workflow (Enamine61 BB, REAL, and MADE, and Mcule59).
